content: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is a condition characterized by the narrowing or blockage of blood vessels that transport blood from the heart to the legs. This condition is most commonly caused by the accumulation of fatty deposits, known as atherosclerosis, within the arterial walls. While PAD can occur in any blood vessel, it is more frequently observed in the arteries of the legs than in the arms. The hallmark symptom of PAD is leg pain during physical activity, such as walking, which typically subsides with rest. However, it is important to note that up to 40% of individuals with PAD may not experience any leg pain. When present, symptoms may include pain, cramping, or aching in the buttocks, hips, thighs, or calves during walking, a condition referred to as claudication. Physical signs that may indicate PAD include muscle weakness or atrophy, loss of hair on the legs, smooth and shiny skin, skin that feels cool to the touch (especially if accompanied by pain during walking that resolves with rest), diminished or absent pulses in the feet, non-healing sores or ulcers on the legs or feet, and cold or numb toes. Several risk factors increase the likelihood of developing PAD. These include smoking, high blood pressure, atherosclerosis, diabetes, high cholesterol levels, and being over the age of 60. Both men and women are affected by PAD, but African Americans are at a higher risk compared to other racial groups. Hispanic individuals may have a similar or slightly elevated risk compared to non-Hispanic White individuals. In the United States, approximately 6.5 million people aged 40 and older are affected by PAD. It is important to recognize that other health conditions and arterial disorders can mimic the symptoms of PAD. Additionally, not all cases of PAD are caused by atherosclerosis. Individuals with PAD are at an increased risk of developing coronary artery disease and cerebrovascular disease, which can lead to heart attacks or strokes. Preventive measures for PAD include engaging in regular physical activity, avoiding tobacco use, and managing risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes. Smoking cessation is particularly critical, as smoking not only increases the risk of PAD but also exacerbates its symptoms. For individuals with PAD, participating in supervised exercise programs can improve symptoms and enhance the ability to walk longer distances. Diagnosis of PAD often involves a noninvasive test called the ankle-brachial index (ABI), which compares blood pressure measurements in the ankles and arms at rest and after exercise. Additional imaging tests, such as ultrasound, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), or computed tomographic (CT) angiography, may also be performed to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment for PAD may include the use of antiplatelet medications, such as aspirin, to prevent complications associated with atherosclerosis. Cholesterol-lowering medications may also be prescribed. Smoking cessation is strongly recommended, and healthcare providers can offer support and resources to help individuals quit smoking. In some cases, surgical intervention, such as bypass surgery, may be necessary to restore blood flow to the affected arteries. Supervised exercise programs are also highly beneficial for individuals experiencing pain due to reduced blood flow to the muscles, as these programs can improve quality of life and alleviate leg symptoms.
